topic: how applications are read / what admissions officers look for
speaker_role: senior college counselor at College Essay Guy; former admissions officer (USC) and former private-school college counseling director, per her own statement
commercial_incentive: Channel sells one-on-one counseling and essay coaching; a promo is included at the end.
key_insights: Holistic review still has a rough academic floor at competitive schools; below it a file is read but unlikely to advance, above it all components are weighed.
She ranks priorities as academic foundation, then character attributes, essays, interest in attending, and recommendations, with test scores omitted because policies are unstable.
Large publics may emphasize quantitative pieces due to volume, while small liberal arts colleges may lean more on qualitative material.
Essay topic matters less than specificity and reflection; a specific everyday topic can beat a generic service-trip story.
Recommendations help most when they add a specific moment or quality, and generic superlatives add little.
Voice that shifts noticeably between personal statement and supplements, suggesting heavy adult polishing, makes a reader question trust.
Applicants from under-resourced backgrounds should explain their circumstances in the additional information section rather than assume the reader knows.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker: average about 12 minutes per file when she read for USC.
Speaker: says a reader may have gone through around 40 applications before yours.
Speaker: composite case study of two similar applicants where the one with a specific, honest story advanced and the one with a generic leadership essay did not.
notable_or_distinctive: The paired composite-applicant comparison makes the specificity-over-impressiveness point concrete, along with the note about mismatched voice.
reliability_notes: Ranking of factors cites her experience and unnamed data from hundreds of colleges without specifics; the case studies are composites.
